## What it is

The Theory of Constraints (TOC) starts from one claim: the throughput of a whole system is governed by a single binding constraint - its bottleneck - and so improving anything other than that constraint does almost nothing for the system as a whole. The durable cognitive move is the **Five Focusing Steps**: (1) **identify** the system's one binding constraint, the step whose limited capacity caps the output of everything downstream; (2) **exploit** it, wringing maximum useful throughput out of that step with the resources already on hand before spending a cent; (3) **subordinate** every other step to that decision, so non-constraints run at the pace the constraint can absorb rather than at their own local maximum; (4) **elevate** the constraint, adding capacity to it only once exploitation is exhausted; and (5) repeat - when the constraint moves, return to step one and **do not let inertia** keep you optimizing yesterday's bottleneck.

The move that does the work is the inversion of ordinary improvement instinct. The default is to make every part faster, cheaper, or more utilized; TOC says that local efficiency at a non-constraint is waste, because a non-bottleneck working harder just builds inventory in front of the bottleneck. The single question it forces is: *what one step limits the throughput of the whole, and is our effort aimed there or scattered?* The deliverable is the named binding constraint plus the exploit / subordinate / elevate decisions attached to it - a single-point intervention plan, not a coverage map.

TOC is broader than this core in practice. Goldratt built operational toolkits on top of it - Drum-Buffer-Rope (DBR) for production scheduling, Critical Chain Project Management (CCPM) for projects, and Throughput Accounting for the money view - plus a separate logic-diagram toolkit, the **Thinking Processes** (Current Reality Tree, Evaporating Cloud / conflict resolution diagram, Future Reality Tree, Prerequisite and Transition Trees), for diagnosing *what to change, what to change to, and how to cause the change*. The registry candidate is scoped to the bottleneck move itself - "find and exploit the system bottleneck" - not to those full operational systems, and that scoping is load-bearing for the evidence grade below.

## When it helps / when it misleads

It helps when a system has a clear **flow** and a plausible single rate-limiter: a delivery pipeline, a manufacturing line, a hiring funnel, a support queue, a CI pipeline, a multi-stage approval. When throughput is capped by one step and teams are spreading improvement effort evenly across all steps, TOC's discipline - find the binding step, squeeze it before buying capacity, and stop optimizing the steps that are not the constraint - is a sharp, useful correction. Its anti-coverage stance is exactly the value: it tells you what to ignore.

It misleads or wastes effort when:

- **There is no single binding constraint, or the constraint is not stable.** TOC assumes one dominant bottleneck governs the system. In problems with several co-equal limiters, a shifting constraint, or no flow at all (a one-off decision, a design question, a values trade-off), forcing a single-constraint frame manufactures a bottleneck that is not really binding and points effort at the wrong place.
- **The problem is about coverage or root cause, not flow.** If the question is "have we considered every category of cause / option?" the right move is exhaustive decomposition, not single-point focus (see `issue-tree`). If it is "why does this keep recurring, and where structurally do we intervene?" the right move is causal depth (see `iceberg-model`). TOC answers neither; it answers "where is the rate-limiting step?"
- **The constraint is treated as found rather than tested.** "Identify the constraint" is a hypothesis. A wrongly named bottleneck - the loudest step rather than the binding one - sends the whole exploit/subordinate/elevate sequence at the wrong target. The method does not itself prove which step is binding; that requires data on each step's capacity versus demand.
- **Local optimization is genuinely the right call.** TOC's "subordinate everything to the constraint" is correct only when one constraint really governs. Applied where it does not, it can justify starving healthy parts of a system to feed a step that was never the true limiter.

## What the evidence says

The honest governing grade is **P (practitioner)**, and the split underneath it is the whole point of this entry.

**What the record supports.** The bottleneck principle is durable, broadly taught, and - unusually for a practitioner method - endorsed even by its critics. Mukherjee and Chatterjee (2007) note that the criticism of Goldratt's work targets his lack of academic rigour and presentation, "but not of the bottleneck approach," treating the two as separate questions. On the *operational* side there is a large descriptive literature: Mabin and Balderstone's review of the international TOC literature (the 2000 book and the 2003 *IJOPM* paper, "The performance of the theory of constraints methodology") aggregated on the order of 80-plus reported TOC applications and found consistent, often large improvements in lead time, inventory, due-date performance, and financial results. Domain reviews echo the pattern: Bacelar-Silva, Cox and Rodrigues (2020), a systematic review of 42 TOC implementations in healthcare, reports positive results across the board - improvements in productivity and timeliness in the large majority of studies - and concludes the evidence "supports TOC as a promising solution." So the supported claim is real and worth stating plainly: in flow-heavy operational settings, focusing improvement on the binding constraint is a sound, repeatedly-reported way to lift system throughput.

**What the record does NOT support.** None of this is controlled, comparative effectiveness evidence for the cognitive move. Two cautions are decisive. First, **selection bias**: Mabin and Balderstone explicitly report finding *no documented failures* in the literature - an outcome that, in a body of self-reported success stories and consulting case studies, signals a literature of winners rather than an unbiased effect estimate, not a method that never fails. Second, **the move under test is not the move in the candidate**: almost all of the operational evidence measures the *full apparatus* - Drum-Buffer-Rope scheduling, Critical Chain, Throughput Accounting - implemented as a management system, not the bare "identify and exploit the bottleneck" reasoning step. The part of TOC closest to a standalone thinking method, the **Thinking Processes / Evaporating Cloud**, has the *weakest* evidence: Kim, Mabin and Davies (2008), reviewing the peer-reviewed Thinking-Processes literature from 1994 to 2006, document how thin the empirical base is, and the broader literature notes there is little to no controlled empirical validation of the Evaporating Cloud's effectiveness in decision-making. So the evidence is genuinely split - **operational TOC: P, with selection-bias caveats; the TOC thinking tools: closer to A/C (anecdotal, conceptually plausible, largely unvalidated)** - and the conservative governing grade is the lower-supported reading of the *actual move*, which is **P**: a durable, operationally-backed principle whose specific cognitive step has no controlled comparative trial. Grading it above P would require borrowing the operational system's case-review record for a reasoning step those studies did not isolate; grading it below P would understate that the bottleneck principle has real, repeated operational backing and near-universal endorsement. P is the honest floor and ceiling.

**Transfer caveat (required).** Every result above is from human teams in manufacturing, projects, and healthcare. None studies a constraint analysis produced by or with an AI agent. The evidence is transferred from human operational practice and is not validated for AI-augmented use; that transfer is a second, independent reason the governing grade is capped at P. A widely-circulated impression that "TOC always works" is itself an artifact of the no-failures-reported literature and must not be read as a measured success rate; it is excluded from the grade and noted here so the absence is on the record.

## Why it is / is not a skill here

Verdict: **Build**, governing tier **P** - confirming, not overturning, the catalog's `cand / build / P` tag, with the distinctness proof made explicit because this method sits *near* the `iceberg-model` boundary and the Build burden of proof has to be discharged, not assumed.

The Build burden is to name a single durable cognitive move that no shipped skill produces, and show that no mode or chain of existing skills yields it. TOC's move is: **treat system throughput as governed by one binding constraint, locate that constraint, and deliberately concentrate effort on it while subordinating (not optimizing) everything else.** Two halves of that are the distinct part: the *anti-coverage* stance (improving a non-constraint is waste) and the *flow/capacity* selection criterion (the binding step is the one whose capacity caps the whole). No shipped skill carries either.

The distinctness proof against the three nearest neighbors:

- **vs `issue-tree` (the breadth tool):** the moves are inverses. Issue-tree decomposes a question into a MECE set of branches precisely so that *nothing* is left uncovered; its discipline is collective exhaustiveness. TOC's discipline is the opposite - find the one step that matters and ignore the rest; coverage is the failure mode, not the goal. Issue-tree has no concept of a binding constraint, of capacity versus demand, or that effort on a non-constraint yields zero system gain. Shared machinery is minimal (both reason over "the parts of a system"); the working mechanism is well under the ~20% ceiling because exhaustive coverage and deliberate single-point focus are opposite selection rules.

- **vs `iceberg-model` (the nearest neighbor - the leverage/where-to-intervene tool):** this is the real test, because iceberg already owns "find the high-leverage place to act" and has *already absorbed* the Meadows leverage-points fold. They differ in the **selection criterion for leverage**. Iceberg/Meadows locates leverage by *causal depth*: descend event -> pattern -> structure -> mental model, on the premise that deeper structural and mindset causes have more leverage. TOC locates leverage by *flow*: the binding constraint is wherever capacity caps throughput, which is frequently a shallow, visible, operational step (a slow review gate, one overloaded engineer, a single machine) with no deep causal or mental-model story at all - and conversely a deep mental-model leverage point is not a "constraint" in TOC's capacity sense. Iceberg has no notion of throughput, capacity, subordination, or "exploit before you elevate." The artifacts differ too: iceberg emits a four-level causal descent; TOC emits a named binding step plus exploit/subordinate/elevate decisions. The conceptual adjacency ("where do we intervene?") is real, which is why this is honestly in the ~20-25% zone rather than far below it - but the mechanism (depth-ladder of causation vs single rate-limiter of flow) is genuinely different, and a pure throughput bottleneck is invisible to the iceberg's four levels. This is the hard wall: **a recurring problem with a deep structural cause goes to `iceberg-model`; a flow capped by one rate-limiting step goes to TOC.** They are complementary, not duplicative.

- **vs `stocks-and-flows-reasoning` (the other flow tool):** both reason about flow, but the moves differ. Stocks-and-flows corrects a specific accumulation error - inferring a stock's direction from a single flow's direction - by separating inflow from outflow and reading the net. TOC does not reason about accumulation trajectory at all; it locates the single rate-limiting step that caps throughput. A bottleneck *is* a flow concept (the slowest step governs the rate), so the adjacency is genuine, but stocks-and-flows has no notion of a binding constraint and TOC has no notion of net-flow accumulation direction. Low-to-medium overlap; different errors corrected.

Why not Fold, Recipe, or Reject. **Fold** fails because the nearest fold target, `iceberg-model`, selects leverage by causal depth and cannot represent the binding-constraint / anti-coverage / capacity-governance move; folding TOC into it would lose exactly the part that is distinct. **Recipe** fails because there is no chain of shipped skills that produces "rank the steps by which one caps system throughput and subordinate the rest" - the library has no constraint, capacity, or throughput primitive, so the move is not assembled from existing parts. **Reject** fails because the move is real, durable, broadly endorsed, and operationally evidenced in its home domain; it is not out of scope (it is a general systems-intervention lens, not a pm-skills domain question) and it is not under-evidenced below the bar (P clears the gate). The learning value of this decision is the mirror image of the Fishbone fold: a famous operational method can still earn a standalone skill *when its distinctive move is a selection principle the catalog does not already own* - here, single-point throughput focus, which neither breadth (issue-tree), depth (iceberg), nor accumulation (stocks-and-flows) provides.

The when-NOT-to-use wall the skill must enforce: do not invent a single bottleneck when none binds or the constraint is unstable; route coverage questions to `issue-tree`, recurring/structural-cause questions to `iceberg-model`, and accumulation-trajectory questions to `stocks-and-flows-reasoning`; and treat the identified constraint as a hypothesis to test against each step's capacity-versus-demand, not as found.

## Lineage and who to read

The Theory of Constraints is **Eliyahu M. Goldratt**'s (1947-2011), an Israeli physicist turned management thinker. He introduced it in 1984 through the business novel *The Goal* (with Jeff Cox), which dramatizes the Five Focusing Steps on a struggling factory and has sold millions of copies as standard operations-management reading. Goldratt extended the core into Critical Chain project management (*Critical Chain*, 1997) and codified the logic-diagram **Thinking Processes** in *What Is This Thing Called Theory of Constraints and How Should It Be Implemented?* (1990). For the honest empirical picture, read Victoria Mabin and Steven Balderstone's review of the international literature (2000 book; 2003 *IJOPM* paper) for the operational case record and its no-failures-reported caveat; Kim, Mabin and Davies (2008) for how thin the Thinking-Processes evidence is; Bacelar-Silva, Cox and Rodrigues (2020) for the healthcare systematic review; and Mukherjee and Chatterjee (2007) for the careful separation of "criticism of Goldratt's rigour" from "criticism of the bottleneck approach." "Theory of Constraints" and "bottleneck analysis" are used generically across the academic and practitioner literature with attribution to Goldratt; the term is not handled here as a trademark, so this entry is documented descriptively with attribution rather than flagged as branded.

### Named sources

- Eliyahu M. Goldratt and Jeff Cox, *The Goal: A Process of Ongoing Improvement* (North River Press, 1984). The founding text; introduces the Five Focusing Steps and the bottleneck principle in narrative form. Foundational / practitioner.
- Eliyahu M. Goldratt, *What Is This Thing Called Theory of Constraints and How Should It Be Implemented?* (North River Press, 1990). Codifies the Thinking Processes logic tools. Primary source.
- Victoria J. Mabin and Steven J. Balderstone, "The performance of the theory of constraints methodology: analysis and discussion of successful TOC applications," *International Journal of Operations & Production Management* 23(6) (2003): 568-595; and *The World of the Theory of Constraints: A Review of the International Literature* (St. Lucie Press, 2000). The most comprehensive review of reported TOC applications; documents large operational/financial improvements and, notably, no reported failures (a selection-bias signal). (P, review of success cases)
- Gabriel M. Bacelar-Silva, James F. Cox III, and Pedro P. Rodrigues, "Outcomes of managing healthcare services using the Theory of Constraints: a systematic review," *Health Systems* 11(1) (2020): 1-16. Systematic review of 42 TOC healthcare implementations; positive outcomes (productivity, timeliness) but a heterogeneous evidence base including non-peer-reviewed sources, no controlled-trial or bias assessment. (P, domain systematic review)
- Sangwon Kim, Victoria J. Mabin, and John Davies, "The theory of constraints thinking processes: retrospect and prospect," *International Journal of Operations & Production Management* 28(2) (2008): 155-184. Reviews the peer-reviewed Thinking-Processes literature (1994-2006) and documents the empirical and publication gaps in the TOC logic tools. (Critical/review literature; bounds the thinking-tools evidence)
- Ashok Mukherjee and A. K. Chatterjee, "Theory of constraints: is it a theory and a good one?" (2007). Separates criticism of Goldratt's academic rigour from the validity of the bottleneck approach itself; useful for not conflating the two. (Critical literature)

> Excluded on the evidence rule: the general impression that "TOC always works," and any implied success rate read off the no-failures-reported literature, trace to a self-selected body of success cases with no controlled comparison; they are not counted toward the grade.
